assumptions.why: the environment holds reset deasserted. Every occupancy contract needs it: reset empties the queue, so 'while full and not reading, the queue stays full' is false across a reset and true under this assumption
the environment supplies an 8-bit payload. Trivially true of the port width, and it is the assumption the data-integrity contract is stated under

contracts.rationale: flag correctness: an empty queue reports empty
flag correctness, the other direction: the flag is not raised while the queue holds data
flag correctness: a queue at capacity reports full
flag correctness: the flag is not raised below capacity
a non-empty queue does not report empty
a queue below capacity does not report full
the occupancy never exceeds the depth. A plain invariant over an output, which is the propositional half of the contract language rather than a template instance
a write into an empty queue leaves exactly one entry, whatever rd_en does (a read while empty is ignored)
the empty flag drops after a write into an empty queue
no underflow effect: without a write the queue stays empty, so a read while empty cannot make the occupancy negative
no overflow effect: without a read the queue stays full, so a write while full cannot grow the occupancy past the depth
the last write fills the queue
a write with no read increments the occupancy. Stated at one occupancy because the general form needs a past operator; the recovery measurement should generalise the family of these into an interval
the last read empties the queue

a simultaneous read and write leaves the queue non-empty: the occupancy does not move. Four propositions in the antecedent, so it is out of reach of a two-slot decision tree and in reach of a three-slot one

data integrity, first-word-fall-through: the value written into an empty queue appears at the output on the next cycle. It is only expressible because the environment holds din for that cycle - an obligation no invariant can state, so it breaks on the stress corpus where din changes every cycle

out_of_grammar.assumption: rst_n == 1 && the environment respects the flags
out_of_grammar.guarantee: the k-th value read equals the k-th value written
out_of_grammar.why_not_minable: first-in-first-out order relates a read to a write that happened an unbounded number of cycles earlier. No template reaches back that far and no past operator exists in the evaluator; FIFO19 is the one-entry case, which is the deepest form the language can state
the general occupancy relation needs $past. FIFO15-17 pin it at individual occupancies instead, which is what a value-equality vocabulary can express

out_of_grammar.guarantee: G(full && wr_en && !rd_en |=> count == 8) and G(empty && rd_en && !wr_en |=> count == 0)
out_of_grammar.why_not_minable: these are true of the RTL and expressible in the grammar, but the nominal environment never writes into a full queue or reads an empty one, so they have zero support on the mining corpus and cannot be confirmed there. They hold with support on the STRESS corpus, which is the one place the reference set is deliberately not validated - a benchmark gap of exactly the kind the CSR error flag has
